old: Its name once simply pointed at a scaly creature, no fangs implied.
In Spanish, the phrase behind it literally means 'the lizard.'
A coincidental Latin word for 'one who binds' may have nudged its final spelling.
clues: This reptile's name began as a Spanish phrase meaning nothing scarier than 'the lizard,' with the little word for 'the' fused right onto the noun.

A big, toothy swamp dweller of the southeastern United States and China, with a broader, rounder snout than a crocodile's. Its spelling was possibly nudged by an unrelated Latin word meaning 'one who binds.'
It finishes the rhyming goodbye 'See you later...', which gets the reply 'In a while, crocodile.' Spanish speakers called the creature el lagarto.
